name: Expense Fraud
title: Expense Fraud
answer: Expense fraud is the deliberate submission of false, inflated, or duplicate expense claims for reimbursement, whether by an employee, a manager, or an outside party working with an insider. It covers fake receipts, personal purchases disguised as business costs, altered invoices, split claims to stay under approval limits, and collusion with vendors. In the field of fraud detection and forensics, the scope includes identifying these schemes, measuring their frequency and cost, and building controls that prevent them. The work sits inside the broader accounting function, where expense reports meet corporate cards, travel bookings, and vendor payments. Detection often begins with a tip or an audit, but the aim is to find patterns before they become losses.

sections.body: Expense fraud is the deliberate submission of false, inflated, or duplicate expense claims for reimbursement, whether by an employee, a manager, or an outside party working with an insider. It covers fake receipts, personal purchases disguised as business costs, altered invoices, split claims to stay under approval limits, and collusion with vendors. In the field of fraud detection and forensics, the scope includes identifying these schemes, measuring their frequency and cost, and building controls that prevent them. The work sits inside the broader accounting function, where expense reports meet corporate cards, travel bookings, and vendor payments. Detection often begins with a tip or an audit, but the aim is to find patterns before they become losses.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Expense fraud detection runs on the same systems that process claims: expense management platforms, enterprise resource planning suites, corporate card feeds, and travel booking tools. These systems produce structured data such as claim amounts, dates, merchant codes, and approval chains, along with unstructured data such as receipt images and email approvals. Detection models and rules typically run in a cloud data warehouse or a dedicated analytics environment, pulling from those sources on a schedule or in real time. Well known platforms in this space include SAP Concur and Expensify, which offer APIs and reporting layers that fraud teams can query. The infrastructure also includes identity and access logs, because who submitted, approved, or changed a claim is often as important as the claim itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with data preparation, joining expense claims to card transactions, travel records, and employee master data. Analysts then apply a mix of deterministic rules, such as duplicate receipt detection or claims just below an approval threshold, and statistical or machine learning models that flag unusual amounts, merchants, or timing. Unsupervised methods like clustering and isolation forests help surface new patterns without labeled examples, while supervised models are trained on past confirmed cases. Graph analysis is used to spot rings of employees or vendors that share addresses, bank accounts, or approval paths. Human investigators review the alerts, gather evidence, and interview subjects, because a model score alone is not proof of fraud.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Expense fraud investigations touch employee privacy, labor law, and data protection rules, so governance must cover what data can be collected, how long it is kept, and who can see it. Provenance matters for both evidence and models: an alert must be traceable to the source claim, the rule or model version that produced it, and the analyst who reviewed it. False positives can harm innocent employees, so organizations often build in review stages, appeal paths, and bias testing for any automated scoring. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect how much of this work sits at the intersection of fraud detection and employment law. Chain of custody for digital evidence, from receipt images to system logs, is essential if a case goes to a disciplinary hearing or court.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous, real-time monitoring rather than periodic audits, with models scoring claims as they are submitted. Generative AI makes it easier to create convincing fake receipts and invoices, so detection tools are being trained to spot synthetic images and inconsistent metadata. At the same time, explainable AI and privacy-preserving techniques are being adopted to satisfy regulators and employee representatives. Integration with corporate card networks and travel platforms is deepening, which allows detection at the point of sale rather than after reimbursement. The long term goal is a control environment where fraud is caught early, evidence is preserved automatically, and legitimate claims are paid without friction.
